title: Gauge R&R for GPU physics engines: can the simulator resolve the policies it ranks?
abstract: In reliability engineering and metrology, 'is the test stimulus itself a trustworthy model' is solved by treating the instrument as a gauge and running a gauge R&R study — repeatability, reproducibility and bias measured on fixed reference items and compared, as %GRR and ndc, to the differences the gauge is used to resolve — before any reading is trusted; carried into L5, that says a GPU-batched physics engine is a gauge whose 'parts' are frozen policies, whose reading is episode return (or per-step state), and whose repeatability (same world, seed, batch slot, repeated), reproducibility (across batch position, batch size, GPU, engine) and bias (against a converged reference step) must be reported as a %GRR against the policy-to-policy return differences people read off it, with ndc telling how many distinguishable policy levels the engine can actually resolve.

sentences: In metrology a measuring instrument (a 'gauge') is characterized before it is trusted by a nested study on a fixed reference item: repeatability is the spread of J back-to-back readings under identical conditions (NIST level 1, pooled s_1 = sqrt(sum s_1lk^2 / LK)), reproducibility is the spread of condition-averages when something is deliberately changed (day, operator, instrument; NIST levels 2 and 3, s_2 and s_3), and the uncertainty of one reading is their combination s_R = sqrt(s_runs^2 + s_days^2 + s_1^2) with s_days = sqrt(s_2^2 - s_1^2/J) and s_runs = sqrt(s_3^2 - s_2^2/K).

Bias is the offset of the gauge's mean reading from a reference of known value and is examined separately from spread, under the headings resolution, linearity, hysteresis, drift and differences among gauges and configurations.

A gauge is accepted only relative to what it must discriminate: AIAG MSA combines repeatability ('equipment variation', EV) and reproducibility ('appraiser variation', AV, appraiser = operator) into GRR, compares it to the variation of the items being measured ('part variation', PV) via %GRR, calls under 10% acceptable, 10-30% marginal and over 30% unacceptable, and requires the number of distinct categories ndc = 1.41 * PV / GRR to be at least 5; the GUM frames the same thing as an uncertainty budget where every component (Type A from repeated observations, Type B from other knowledge) is listed and combined into one standard uncertainty.
sources: https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/mpc/section4/mpc44.htm — NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 2.4.4 'How do we quantify variability of measurements?' (nested design, s_1/s_2/s_3, s_R formula; fetched)

https://help.sigmazone.com/quantum-xl/v17/statistical-tools/msa/msa-statistics — MSA statistics page citing AIAG MSA Reference Manual 3rd ed. p.77 (%GRR thresholds 10/30) and p.117 (ndc = 1.41*PV/GRR, ndc >= 5) (fetched; the AIAG manual itself is paywalled)
https://doi.org/10.59161/JCGM100-2008E — JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data — Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (GUM) (landing page fetched; abstract only)

import_sentence: In reliability engineering and metrology, 'is the test stimulus itself a trustworthy model' is solved by treating the instrument as a gauge and running a gauge R&R study — repeatability, reproducibility and bias measured on fixed reference items and compared, as %GRR and ndc, to the differences the gauge is used to resolve — before any reading is trusted; carried into L5, that says a GPU-batched physics engine is a gauge whose 'parts' are frozen policies, whose reading is episode return (or per-step state), and whose repeatability (same world, seed, batch slot, repeated), reproducibility (across batch position, batch size, GPU, engine) and bias (against a converged reference step) must be reported as a %GRR against the policy-to-policy return differences people read off it, with ndc telling how many distinguishable policy levels the engine can actually resolve.

predicts.statement: For deterministic frozen policies on contact-rich GPU-simulated tasks (e.g., in-hand cube rotation, quadruped on rough terrain in Isaac Lab / MJX / Genesis), the engine-only gauge variance of episode return — repeatability plus reproducibility across batch size and batch position, with the policy and initial state held fixed — gives %GRR above 30% against the return gaps (3-10%) that papers report as method improvements, and ndc below 5; on smooth tasks (e.g., cartpole, flat-ground locomotion) %GRR is below 10%.
predicts.expected: Judgment, not evidence: probability 0.6 that at least one of three contact-rich tasks shows %GRR > 30% at batch sizes >= 4096 with default iteration caps, and that the engine-gauge component accounts for 20-50% of what papers call 'seed variance' (the std over training seeds); bias against a converged reference (finer dt, more solver iterations) exceeds the repeatability band on the contact-rich tasks, i.e., the engine is precise but inaccurate where it is precise and both imprecise and inaccurate where contact dominates.
predicts.field_assumes: Robot-RL practice treats the simulator as a noiseless oracle: variance is reported over training seeds and attributed to learning; GPUSimBench documents run-to-run and inter-environment variability as a reproducibility concern, not as a measurement-resolution limit, and no engine ships a repeatability/reproducibility/bias specification or a minimum resolvable return difference.
predicts.would_change: If %GRR of the engine alone exceeds 30% against reported method gaps on any widely used task, then a share of published 'A beats B by 5%' results on that task are gauge noise and every leaderboard built on that engine needs a resolution floor (ndc) column; if instead %GRR < 10% everywhere and bias sits inside the repeatability band, the belief 'GPU non-determinism matters for conclusions' is killed with a number and the lane's audit can drop the batch-slot axis.

identifiability: Random given: fixed engine build, fixed GPU model, fixed batch size and batch slot, fixed seed, fixed initial state, fixed policy run with deterministic actions (argmax / mean action; temperature 0 so the policy contributes zero decision variance by construction). What remains in the repeatability term is only the engine's floating-point reduction order under GPU thread scheduling — a property of the engine+hardware system, not of the protocol. Reproducibility factors (batch position, batch size, GPU model, engine) are chosen and crossed by the experimenter, so the reproducibility term is a property of the engine family under the stated factor ranges and must be reported with those ranges. Bias is defined against a named reference step (CPU double precision, dt/4, uncapped Newton iterations) and is a property of the engine configuration, not of the policy. The 'parts' (policies) are fixed checkpoints, so PV is well-defined and no training randomness enters; if a stochastic policy were used instead, policy temperature would be confounded with gauge noise and the quantity would not be identifiable.

probe.design: Three tasks spanning contact regimes (one smooth, two contact-rich) in one engine (Isaac Lab/PhysX or MJX; Genesis as second engine if time allows). 'Parts': 10 frozen checkpoints per task spanning a return range, run with deterministic actions. Fixed set of 50 initial states per task. Nested/crossed design following NIST 2.4.4: repeatability = 10 repeats at the same batch slot and batch size; reproducibility factors = batch position (first, middle, last slot), batch size (64, 1024, 8192), GPU model (2); bias = the same (x_t, u_t) re-stepped under the converged reference (the lane's d_t audit) and summarized as mean return offset. Fit variance components (ANOVA / pooled standard deviations), compute s_R, GRR, PV, %GRR = GRR / sqrt(GRR^2 + PV^2), ndc = 1.41 PV/GRR, and %GRR-to-tolerance with tolerance = the smallest return gap claimed as an improvement in the task's three most-cited papers. Output: a one-page gauge R&R card per engine x task, plus the share of published seed-std attributable to the gauge.
probe.cost: About 10 policies x 50 states x 10 repeats x 3 slots x 3 batch sizes x 2 GPUs = 90k episodes per task, trivially batched: under 30 GPU-hours total including the CPU reference re-steps; 4-6 days of one person including checkpoint collection.
probe.kills_if: On all three tasks, at every batch size and slot, %GRR against the published method gaps is below 10%, ndc >= 5, and the bias against the converged reference lies inside the repeatability band — the engine is an acceptable gauge for the differences people claim, GPU non-determinism is a reproducibility nuisance and not a resolution limit, and the import is dead. Also dead if the engine is bitwise deterministic at fixed batch configuration and all remaining variance is a pure batch-size effect, because that reduces to what GPUSimBench already reported.

papers.title: GPUSimBench: Towards Scalable and Reliable GPU-Accelerated Simulators in Embodied AI
papers.trick: Runs Isaac Lab and Genesis on an inclined-plane task and scaling sweeps, and shows that identical initial conditions produce different trajectories run-to-run and across environment slots in the batch, sorting the causes into four regimes of stochasticity.
papers.did_not: Did not separate the variance into nested repeatability / reproducibility / bias components with a design, did not compare the engine's variance to the policy-return differences it is used to resolve (%GRR, ndc), did not measure bias against a converged reference, and did not ask how many distinguishable policy levels the engine can rank.

papers.title: On the Numerical Reliability of Differentiable Physics-Based Optimization for Robotic Material Manipulation
papers.trick: On two Material-Point-Method system-identification benchmarks, shows that GPU reductions whose order depends on thread scheduling flip the sign of long-horizon gradients, and that repeated-run loss variation grows faster with horizon than the loss change caused by the parameter perturbation being tested.

title: pass^k is one point on a survival curve; report the hazard over steps
abstract: In reliability engineering, 'how reliable is this unit' is answered by estimating the survival function and the hazard rate over operating time from failure-time data with censoring, and reading the failure mechanism off the hazard's shape (falling = born broken, flat = memoryless, rising = wear-out); carried into L1, that says an agent's pass^k on a task is the k-th power of one point of a survival curve over steps, R(T)^k at the step budget T, and that the field should report R(t) and the hazard h(t) over turns or tool calls with budget-exhausted runs marked censored, because two agents or two model versions with equal pass^k can have opposite hazard shapes (fail-at-the-fork early vs degrade late), which pass^k cannot distinguish and which call for different fixes.

sentences: Reliability is not a number but a curve: the survival function R(t) is the probability a unit is still working at time t, and the quantity that characterizes it is the hazard h(t) = f(t)/R(t), which NIST defines as 'the (instantaneous) rate of failure for the survivors' at t; the two are tied by H(t) = -ln R(t), so the whole hazard curve, not one reliability figure, is the object the field estimates.

The shape of the hazard over life names the failure mechanism: the 'bathtub' has an early period 'characterized by a high but rapidly decreasing failure rate' (infant mortality, units that were broken from the start), a long flat middle where 'the failure rate levels off and remains roughly constant', and a late rise 'as materials wear out'; the Weibull model indexes all three with one shape number gamma through h(t) = (gamma/alpha)(t/alpha)^(gamma-1) (falling for gamma<1, constant for gamma=1 where it 'reduces to the Exponential Model', rising for gamma>1).

Units still running when the test stops are censored, not failed ('When not all units on test fail we have censored data'): Type I when the test stops at a fixed time, interval ('readout') when only a window containing the failure is known, and every unit yields 'exactly one of' a run-time without failure, an exact failure time, or an interval; separately, a measuring instrument (gauge) is trusted only after a gauge R&R study quantifies its repeatability (short-term, same conditions), reproducibility (day-to-day) and stability (run-to-run) variability.
sources: https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/apr/section1/apr123.htm — NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 8.1.2.3 'Failure (or hazard) rate' (also 8.1.2.2 'Reliability or survival function', 8.1.2.4 'Bathtub curve' https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/apr/section1/apr124.htm, 8.1.6.2 'Weibull' https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/apr/section1/apr162.htm, 8.1.3.1 'Censoring' https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/apr/section1/apr131.htm)

https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/mpc/section4/mpc44.htm — NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook 2.4.4 'How do we quantify variability of measurements?' (Level 1 repeatability/short-term, Level 2 reproducibility/day-to-day, Level 3 stability/run-to-run); 2.4.1 'Issues for a gauge R&R study' https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/mpc/section4/mpc41.htm

import_sentence: In reliability engineering, 'how reliable is this unit' is answered by estimating the survival function and the hazard rate over operating time from failure-time data with censoring, and reading the failure mechanism off the hazard's shape (falling = born broken, flat = memoryless, rising = wear-out); carried into L1, that says an agent's pass^k on a task is the k-th power of one point of a survival curve over steps, R(T)^k at the step budget T, and that the field should report R(t) and the hazard h(t) over turns or tool calls with budget-exhausted runs marked censored, because two agents or two model versions with equal pass^k can have opposite hazard shapes (fail-at-the-fork early vs degrade late), which pass^k cannot distinguish and which call for different fixes.

predicts.statement: On tau-bench retail tasks whose pass^1 lies in [0.25, 0.75] (the 'coin-flip' tasks) with k=8 runs per task and an open-weight agent, the step of first unrecoverable error (located by a judge, audited by counterfactual forking on a subset) has a non-constant hazard: a discrete-time Weibull fit gives a shape gamma whose 95% interval excludes 1 in at least 50% of these tasks, and the sign of gamma-1 splits the coin-flip tasks into two clusters (early-fork, gamma<1; wear-out, gamma>1) that are indistinguishable by pass^1 or pass^8. Second clause: runs that end by hitting the turn or token budget make up at least 10% of recorded failures for at least one model, and scoring them as censored instead of failed moves pass^8 by at least 3 points.
predicts.expected: Judgment: both clusters exist and the early-fork cluster is the majority (roughly 60/40), because tau-bench failures concentrate at one or two policy-interpretation turns near the start of the conversation, with a wear-out minority driven by self-conditioning on earlier errors (the mechanism 2509.09677 reports: 'models become more likely to make mistakes when the context contains their errors from prior turns').
predicts.field_assumes: The lane treats a task as a Bernoulli coin with one success probability p and reports pass^k = p^k (tau-bench 2406.12045 proposes pass^k 'to evaluate the reliability of agent behavior over multiple trials'); where a time axis is used at all, a constant per-step hazard is assumed (Ord 2505.05115: 'a constant rate of failing during each minute a human would take to do the task'; 2509.09677 compounds a per-step accuracy), and budget-exhausted runs are counted as failures, never as censored.
predicts.would_change: If the shape clusters exist, a leaderboard column changes: pass^k is supplemented by (R(t) curve, gamma, censored share) per task family, and 'version A is more reliable than version B' becomes a statement about which part of the curve moved. If instead gamma=1 holds almost everywhere, that is the citable negative: the constant-hazard model that Ord fit across tasks also holds within runs, pass^k is a sufficient statistic for agent reliability, and the lane's point-estimate habit is vindicated for the first time with evidence rather than convention.

identifiability: Random given the task, the agent's sampling temperature, the user simulator's temperature and the tool environment's stochasticity; a temperature-0 agent on a deterministic environment with a fixed-seed simulator has a step-function survival curve and no hazard to estimate, so the hazard is a property of the agent-plus-protocol system at the stated temperatures, not of the agent alone (tau-bench's user simulator contributes failures of its own; the probe's second kill clause measures that share). The failure time is not directly observed: the terminal step is a detection time, and the first unrecoverable step is located either by a judge (noisy; judge and verifier are different objects, the judge here is the locator and the database-state check is the verifier) or by counterfactual forking (the step after which resampled continuations succeed with probability below 0.1), which makes the observed data interval-censored failure times in the field's own terms; the estimand is the hazard over steps for the system under the stated protocol, and budget exhaustion is Type I censoring at T.

probe.design: tau-bench retail + airline (165 tasks) x 8 runs with one open-weight agent (e.g. Qwen3-32B class) and the standard GPT-class user simulator at tau-bench's default temperatures; log every turn and tool call. For each failed run record (a) the terminal turn, (b) the judge-located first unrecoverable turn (LLM judge with a 50-run human audit, agreement reported), (c) on 20 coin-flip tasks x 4 runs, counterfactual forks (4 continuations) every 3rd turn to locate the step where success probability drops below 0.1, as the gold standard against the judge. Mark budget-exhausted runs as right-censored. Fit per task a discrete-time Weibull (and a nonparametric Kaplan-Meier curve) to failure-step data; test gamma=1 by likelihood ratio against the constant-hazard (geometric) model; recompute pass^8 with censored runs excluded vs counted as failures. Second analysis: at each located failure step, resample only the user simulator's turn (4 draws) and record how often the outcome flips.
probe.cost: About 1,320 full episodes plus about 1,600 partial fork episodes: roughly $300-600 in API spend for the user simulator and judge plus about 60 GPU-hours (one 8xH100 node for a day) to serve the agent; 5 working days including the audit.
probe.kills_if: Dead if, across coin-flip tasks, the 95% interval for gamma contains 1 in 80% or more of tasks AND the likelihood-ratio test rejects the constant-hazard model in fewer than 20% of tasks: then the failure-step distribution carries no information beyond its mean and pass^k is sufficient. Reassigned to S1 (variance attribution), not an L1 reliability claim, if resampling only the user simulator's turn at the located failure step flips the outcome in more than 50% of cases: the hazard is then a property of the simulator. The censoring clause dies on its own if budget-exhausted runs are under 5% of failures for every model.

consumers.action_changed: Add a per-task-family reliability curve (R(t) over turns, Weibull shape gamma, censored-run share) next to pass^k, and stop scoring budget-exhausted runs as failures without a flag.

Choose the fix by hazard shape: a falling hazard (early-fork) says put RL credit and prompting effort on the first few turns; a rising hazard (wear-out) says schedule compaction or a restart at the hazard knee, the agent analogue of preventive replacement in reliability engineering (replace before the wear-out rise).

consumers.action_changed: Replace the constant-hazard assumption in horizon extrapolation with the fitted shape; a gamma different from 1 within tasks changes the predicted success rate at longer task lengths and therefore the horizon-doubling estimate.

title: Per-task success as a drifting hidden state: observability and innovation tests for version change
abstract: In control theory and state estimation, reliability across versions is the problem of tracking a hidden state (each task's success probability in logit units) from noisy measurements (k binary run outcomes) and is solved by observability (the measurement structure fixes which functions of the hidden state are recoverable at all) plus the innovation test (compare each new measurement with the filter's prediction; the surprises are white with the predicted covariance when the model is right); carried into L1, that says a benchmark owner should treat each version's per-task results as innovations against a per-task tracker, and read a benchmark or harness change as a measurement-equation fault (innovations correlated across tasks that share the changed harness component, and flips of near-deterministic tasks) rather than as a state drift of the agent.

sentences: Observability: a hidden state can be recovered from the record of measurements if and only if the observability matrix (the stack C, CA, ..., CA^(n-1), where C is the measurement map and A the state transition) has full column rank; any state direction in its null space produces the same outputs as zero, and in the lecture notes' words 'no signal processing of any kind applied to u and y can deduce x' in that direction.

Innovation: the innovation is the measurement minus the filter's predicted measurement; when the filter's model and noise statistics are right, the normalized innovation sequence 'is a white Gaussian noise with zero mean and identity covariance matrix' (Mehra and Peschon 1971, as quoted by Hajiyev 2008), and with white measurement noise the innovations are white if and only if the process-noise model is right (IWAKF, arXiv 2604.21644).

Diagnostic: comparing the sample covariance or autocorrelation of the innovations with their predicted values detects a wrong model or a sensor fault online; which measurement channels' innovations move, and whether they stay correlated over time, is the evidence for which part of the model is wrong (Hajiyev tests the innovation covariance trace against identity for aircraft sensor faults).
sources: https://stanford.edu/class/ee363/lectures/observ.pdf — EE363 Lecture 5, 'Observability and state estimation' (Stanford, Winter 2008-09): observability matrix, rank condition, unobservable subspace, least-squares observer under noise

https://skoge.folk.ntnu.no/prost/proceedings/ifac2008/data/papers/0071.pdf — C. Hajiyev, 'Testing the Covariance Matrix of the Innovation Sequence in Application to Aircraft Sensor Fault Detection', IFAC World Congress 2008 (cites Mehra and Peschon 1971 for the white zero-mean identity-covariance property of normalized innovations)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.21644 — 'An Adaptive Kalman Filter that Learns the Coloring Dynamics of the Process Noise' (2026): innovations white iff process noise white, given white measurement noise

Blocked (permission not granted in time): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8638515 — 'On the Identification of Noise Covariances and Adaptive Kalman Filtering: A New Look at a 50 Year-Old Problem' (abstract only via Authorea: identifiability of Q and R from innovation auto/cross-covariances is 'in dispute' and rests on a rank condition)

import_sentence: In control theory and state estimation, reliability across versions is the problem of tracking a hidden state (each task's success probability in logit units) from noisy measurements (k binary run outcomes) and is solved by observability (the measurement structure fixes which functions of the hidden state are recoverable at all) plus the innovation test (compare each new measurement with the filter's prediction; the surprises are white with the predicted covariance when the model is right); carried into L1, that says a benchmark owner should treat each version's per-task results as innovations against a per-task tracker, and read a benchmark or harness change as a measurement-equation fault (innovations correlated across tasks that share the changed harness component, and flips of near-deterministic tasks) rather than as a state drift of the agent.

predicts.statement: On version-to-version transitions where the cause is known (a model release with the harness frozen, versus a harness, tool or judge change with the model pinned), the innovation vector's structure (share of flips on tasks with estimated p outside [0.1, 0.9]; correlation of innovations along harness-component groupings versus along difficulty bands) classifies the cause with AUC above 0.9 without using the pinned control arm.
predicts.expected: Judgment, probability 0.65: model releases also flip near-deterministic tasks (regressions are documented in 2307.09009: GPT-4 prime/composite 84% to 51% between March and June 2023), so the flip signature does not separate the two causes; AUC lands between 0.6 and 0.75 and the control arm stays necessary.
predicts.field_assumes: L1 today assumes the pinned control arm (re-run the old model on the new harness) is the separation device, and it is; and it already reads k runs through pass^k, which is exactly E_i[p_i^k], the k-th moment of the per-task success distribution — the full content of what k binary runs can observe about the task-level distribution.
predicts.would_change: An AUC above 0.9 would give closed-API benchmarks whose old versions are deprecated (no control arm possible) a who-moved detector from outcomes alone; that would add a column to HAL-style leaderboards. Our expected result makes the detector a footnote: 'innovation structure does not separate model from harness change on N labeled transitions.'

identifiability: Random given the task set, the harness version, the model version, and the sampling settings (temperature and seed) of the agent, of any simulated user and of any judge. From k runs of task i under version v, the recoverable functions of the hidden per-task state are exactly the moments E[p_i^j] for j <= k (binomial-mixture identifiability); with the standard k = 1 per task the per-task state is unobservable and only the task average is observable, and distinguishing 'coin-flip' tasks (p near 0.5) from 'bimodal' tasks (p near 0 or 1) needs k >= 2 (second moment 0.25 versus 0.5). At temperature 0 with a deterministic harness every p_i is 0 or 1 and the remaining run-to-run noise belongs to the harness, simulated user and judge, so the tracked quantity is a property of the protocol (agent + harness + judge), not of the agent alone. pass^k is this moment sequence under its lane name.

probe.design: Use public multi-version agent results with both arms present: SWE-bench Verified runs across harness fixes with pinned models and across model releases with pinned harness (the 60,000-trajectory set of 2602.07150 is a candidate source), and tau-bench to tau2-bench transitions. Fit a logit random-walk tracker per task (process noise per transition, binomial measurement with k runs), form the innovation vector per transition, compute (a) share of flips on tasks with estimated p outside [0.1, 0.9], (b) correlation of innovations within harness-component groups (shared tool, repo, judge) versus within difficulty bands, and classify known model-change versus harness-change transitions by these two features. Baseline: the pinned-control-arm answer, which is exact wherever the arm exists.
probe.cost: No new training; $0 to $200 of API if two versions x 200 tasks x 5 runs are re-run for one benchmark; 3 to 5 days of one person; zero GPU-hours.
probe.kills_if: Classification AUC below 0.7 on at least six labeled transitions, or if in every real case a pinned control arm was available (then the detector has no consumer). Both outcomes are footnotes: 'innovation structure cannot tell a model release from a harness change at this k', or 'the control arm is always available, use it'.

title: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use
abstract: For AI assistants to move beyond simple chat interfaces and reliably assist users with applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack, we need to improve their tool-use capabilities. However, existing tool use benchmarks are still limited and difficult to scale because they rely on human supervision or are too domain-specific. To make data generation scalable, we propose, TURTLE (Tool Use Related Tasks with Long-Horizon Evolution), an Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approach to evolve existing tasks using a proposer, a solver, and a feedback generator large language model agents. The proposer is rewarded for difficult yet solvable tasks based on the solver's empirical performance, and the feedback generator summarizes the solver's execution traces for the proposer to exploit. TURTLE produces evolving, self-tuning test suites adaptable to different environment requirements, from supporting user simulators and dense document retrieval to interacting across multiple apps. Empirical results on AppWorld, $τ$-Bench, and AutomationBench using Gemma 4 31B-it show that the evolved tasks target the desired difficulty range (e.g., a 165% increase in the percentage of hard tasks on AppWorld), increase task diversity (in terms of reasoning and simultaneous tool interactions), and elicit a broader range of failure modes than the original tasks.
triage_reason: Self-tuning task generator targeting a difficulty band on AppWorld and tau-Bench; enabling piece for benchmark saturation and churn, not a static set.

title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
abstract: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls shows that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy.
triage_reason: Measures where keeping tool output out of context loses accuracy (evidence substitution), simulation held fixed; L4 context-management measurement

title: When the harness decides success: state that cannot be re-observed
abstract: Agent harnesses decide what a language model sees across turns: they drop old turns, summarize them, or replay the model's own earlier reasoning. We ask when these choices change whether an agent succeeds, not only what it costs, and report three findings. First, in a pre-registered synthetic probe, truncating the context window costs a low-cost reasoning model nothing in success when a needed fact can be looked up again (it looks the fact up instead), but drops its success to chance when the fact cannot be re-observed: the two penalties differ by 92.5 percentage points (90% CI [89.5, 95.5]). A pre-registered replication on one model from a second provider showed the same contrast. Once the fact was lost, that model chose no answer rather than guessing. Second, on ARC-AGI-3, where the benchmark's Standard harness trails its Provider Adapter harness by a wide margin, we decompose that gap one component at a time, for one model on four games. Summarizing old turns instead of dropping them, while keeping the Standard harness's invitation to take notes, recovers 86% of a 63-point gap without replaying the model's reasoning. The same harness without the invitation recovers 43%, and adding the provider's native replay of the model's reasoning recovers the remaining 57%. These are point estimates from one counted run per configuration and game, and the replay share depends on a single run. Third, in the benchmark's published runs and in ours, the Adapter's advantage in the probability of clearing a level it has reached is larger at deep levels than at early ones. This largely restates where runs stopped and does not separate a growing advantage from a constant one.
triage_reason: Pre-registered probe: truncation costs nothing when facts are re-observable, chance when not; decomposes a harness gap component by component

title: When Coding Agents Outpace Review: Evaluating PRD-Driven Development in Mature Enterprise Repositories
abstract: Coding agents increasingly undertake development tasks in mature enterprise repositories, yet existing benchmarks offer limited insight into whether they fulfill complete Product Requirement Documents (PRDs) and where delivery breaks down. Issue resolution and development from scratch leave incremental PRD fulfillment underexplored, while isolated tests provide incomplete evidence of business and integration requirements. We introduce PACE, a benchmark of 43 enterprise tasks with 750 expert-audited Code Points. It combines requirement reconstruction, criterion construction, and evidence-based evaluation to measure PRD fulfillment and connect delivery gaps to agent behavior. Across 11 model--scaffold configurations, most scores fall between 52.1 and 78.1; GPT-5.6-Sol achieves the highest complete-delivery rate of 14.0\%. Incomplete implementation and missing integration are the principal bottlenecks: producing individual components does not ensure a complete delivery. Evaluation achieves 95.2\% agreement with expert consensus, with lower case-level variation across judging records than repeated executions. Beyond model comparison, the benchmark provides actionable feedback for harness refinement: diagnosis guides targeted improvements, and successive harness releases raise mean performance from 59.4 to 63.0 using the same model and task suite. Code is available at https://github.com/TianqiLiu1/PACE-Bench.

title: Beyond Behavioral Accuracy: Evaluating Individual-Level Fidelity in LLM Investor Simulation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as user simulators, but can they faithfully reproduce an individual's behavior and decision logic over time? We investigate this question in a longitudinal paper-trading study with 80 participants. Using rolling next-day predictions, we evaluate trading activity, buy-sell structure, asset selection, and portfolio outcomes, complemented by controlled input ablations and participant-rated explanation alignment. No evaluated LLM reliably outperforms a simple recent-activity persistence baseline for predicting trade occurrence, while buy-sell structure and asset selection remain difficult to reproduce. Similar activity-level performance can also yield substantially different portfolio trajectories. Ablations show that activity predictions depend primarily on recent trades, whereas asset choices are sensitive to multiple evidence sources. Participants rate explanations as more aligned with their recurring strategies than with their decision-specific rationales. These findings reveal a gap between coarse behavioral agreement and individual-level fidelity, motivating separate evaluation of behavioral accuracy, explanation alignment, and evidence dependence in personalized user simulation.

title: Can LLM User-Proxies Stand In for Humans in Reliance Measurement? Replicating Rel-A.I. with Simulated Users
abstract: Can language-model user proxies reproduce human reliance on an AI answer across contexts? Published simulated-user studies do not establish validity for this partial-answer decision, and Rel-A.I.'s released human record omits trial-level choices. We audit its 90 printed questions and 15 domain-by-marker reliance rates using sampled decisions and counterbalanced A/B probabilities from open models through 72B parameters. A matched crossover varies the printed agent specialty within each question, separating question content, label averages, and their interaction. Mistral Small's strong-marker math-minus-law label marginal is -0.4 percentage points, yet matching the agent label to the question domain raises reliance by 13.3 points on average across the five domains. The best A/B proxy has 22.5-point absolute-rate error and 8.3-point domain-effect error against the human table. A two-sample independent-binomial human replication has 3.5-point expected domain-effect error under the stated working model. The interaction is model dependent, and inference layout changes identical-prompt probabilities. This single-study audit does not establish proxy validity for human effect sizes or general directional screening.

title: Vulnerability Analysis for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement
abstract: Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (SMARL) aims to learn cooperative control policies under prescribed safety constraints. Al- though existing SMARL methods focus on enforcing safety during policy optimization, their vulnerability remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates inference-time observation attacks against SMARL, where an adversary perturbs the observations of a subset of agents, thereby altering the actions produced by their policies. We propose MinMax Attack, an attack framework that jointly selects adversarial target actions for compromised agents while accounting for the Cooperative Resistance of benign agents. We further derive a bound on the induced safety cost and characterize its relation- ship with the Compromised-Agent Budget and the Perturbation Budget. Experiments across multiple safety-critical multi-agent benchmarks and representative state-of-the-art SMARL algorithms show that MinMax Attack induces substantially higher safety costs than existing attack baselines while preserving task reward, thereby reducing its detectability and achieving both attack effectiveness and stealthiness.

title: Train An Imaginative Agent
abstract: A seemingly reasonable push in Sokoban can make the puzzle unsolvable. To avoid such mistakes, an agent has to anticipate the consequences of its actions before execution, especially when feedback from the real environment is sparse or actions are irreversible. We introduce Agentic Imagination (Agima), a training framework that trains an agent to imagine before acting, i.e. to be imaginative. Agima trains a single omni model to propose actions, generate images of their outcomes, and then reason over these imagined futures to decide what to execute in the real environment. Rather than committing to a single plan, the agent can simulate a sequence of actions, explore alternatives, and compare possible futures. We first use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to unify policy and world modeling within a single omni model. This enables the agent to predict future outcomes and perform basic forms of imagination, such as forward thinking and counterfactual branching. We then use agentic reinforcement learning (RL) to teach the agent to reason with its imagined futures and use them effectively for planning. Across four environments spanning Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, Agima generalizes to harder settings unseen during training. Trained with SFT alone on two-box Sokoban, Agima solves 40% of four-box puzzles while seeing the real board only once every five moves, compared with an action-only planner that only solves 2%. After RL, new behaviors emerge in how Agima uses its imagination: it learns a new unified format that was unseen during the SFT stage, learns to conduct forward thinking only when necessary, and branches more frequently at critical decision points. An agent that can picture where its actions lead can learn when and where to look ahead, that is, to plan. Project page: https://agima.net/.

title: VaDar: Implicit Goal Conditioning via Value Disaggregation
abstract: Long-horizon tasks are important for modern AI and robotics, yet pose a challenge for reinforcement learning. Historically, a popular approach has been to decompose a task into subgoals, and learn a subgoal-conditioned policy to execute each subtask in sequence. We introduce an alternative called Value Disaggregation (VaDar), which trains a single subgoal-independent policy to maximize a linear combination of per-subgoal critic values. Because subgoal information is needed only at training-time, VaDar removes the need for possibly costly or cumbersome subgoal-selection during policy deployment. Moreover, through careful experiments, we show that VaDar (1) is always competitive with, and frequently outperforms, natural baselines like goal-conditioning and (2) succeeds on tasks with non-sequential goal structure and multiple optimization objectives. In particular, VaDar is the first algorithm to solve challenging, long-horizon tasks in the RoboCasa suite, even when starting from a policy pretrained from behavior cloning with near-zero initial task success. Taken together, VaDar's successes suggest that subgoal information benefits actor-critic reinforcement learning by enhancing the efficacy of critic learning, whereas policy goal-conditioning is often unnecessary.

title: Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions
abstract: Despite recent advances in policy learning, long-horizon manipulation remains difficult because learned policies must avoid compounding errors while preserving future feasibility. While search-based planning can explicitly reason over such future consequences, it quickly becomes expensive in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. This raises a central question: how can long-horizon reasoning from search be transferred into policies in continuous action spaces? To this end, we propose DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation to generate long-horizon plans. During search, a learned policy proposes continuous actions, while a learned value function scores actions by their expected progress toward task completion. Using GPU-parallelized simulation, DISCO periodically distills MCTS-generated plans into the policy-value model, improving the action proposals and value estimates used in subsequent searches. Finally, the learned policy-value model can be directly deployed without the need for simulator-based search at test time. Across simulated and real-world rearrangement tasks, DISCO outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines.

title: ToolOPD: Credit-Aware On-Policy Distillation for Tool-Use Agents
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) enhances the capabilities of small language agents by providing dense, token-level supervision from a teacher model on student-generated trajectories. However, standard OPD implicitly assumes that credit is uniformly distributed across long-horizon trajectories, assigning the same strength of teacher supervision to different actions. Through credit-distribution analysis and outcome-reversal counterfactual experiments, we find that trajectory credit is concentrated on a small number of critical actions. Moreover, even when the trajectory is held fixed, reversing only the final outcome substantially changes the credit assigned to multiple interaction turns. These findings show that the uniform-credit assumption fails to identify critical decisions and ultimately degrades the model's reasoning accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose ToolOPD, an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework designed for long-horizon tool use. ToolOPD first summarizes each completed trajectory and its outcome into a reusable hindsight skill. It then measures how this skill changes the teacher's probability of each student action token and converts the change into outcome-aware credit. The resulting credit preserves supervision that supports successful decisions or discourages failed ones, while suppressing irrelevant and conflicting signals. ToolOPD uses these credits to reweight the action-level distillation loss and jointly optimizes it with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across multiple long-horizon tool interaction benchmarks demonstrate that ToolOPD significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines.
triage_reason: OPD-RL hybrid with hindsight-skill credit reweighting; retired theme T2 territory and a recipe; the credit-concentration analysis is its only L2 touch.

title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap, they mostly rely on knowledge reuse or summarization, an approach that is often constrained by directly retrieval without any adaptation for the current task, while the retrieved memory may contain much history noises waiting to be preprocessed. In contrast, MAS characterized by task-specific guidance often lack long-term memory specifically designed for the guidance. To address these challenges, we propose M-Plan, a closed-loop MAS framework that integrates long-term and short-term memory. By combining global-local and past-current guidance, M-Plan enhances agents' performance on multi-turn tasks while maintaining a plug-and-play design. During task execution, agents receive task-specific milestones and insights, and are provided with local hints only when confusion arises, which form global-local guidance together. These guidance generation and utilization construct the short-term memory as well. After task completion, relevant information about the current task is optimized or reorganized before being sent to the long-term memory storage for future retrieval. The designments mentioned above build a comprehensive framework different from other individual long-term or short-term memory works. Extensive experiments on multi-turn tasks including ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models demonstrate that M-Plan outperforms multiple baseline methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

title: Learning Who Talks to Whom: Role-Aware Communication Topology Scheduling for Efficient LLM Multi-Agent Collaboration
abstract: Multi-agent systems driven by large language models (LLMs) rely on structured communication topologies to facilitate information exchange and collaborative reasoning. However, effectively scheduling these topologies to dynamically determine who talks to whom and when to communicate remains a fundamental challenge in balancing collective reasoning performance against exponential token overhead. Existing topology scheduling approaches either enforce static communication graphs that cannot adapt to dynamic problem-solving states, or overlook agent role complementarity while failing to explicitly incorporate the synthesized graph structure into team-level decision evaluation. To tackle these limitations, we propose ACTS, a role-aware adaptive communication topology scheduling framework for efficient LLM multi-agent collaboration. Orchestrated within a Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm, ACTS introduces a novel dual-attention mechanism. Specifically, a Role-conditioned Relational Attention module dynamically selects variable-cardinality interaction partners based on agent roles and evolving execution states, while a Topological Attention Mixer explicitly embeds the directed communication topology into team value decomposition for precise credit assignment. Comprehensive evaluations across 9 challenging benchmarks covering code generation, multi-step reasoning, general knowledge, and competitive mathematics demonstrate that ACTS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, boosting average accuracy by up to 6.19 percentage points while reducing token consumption by over 15%. The project website is available at https://acts-mas.github.io/ACTS/.

title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.

title: Map-Distribution Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
abstract: Designing capable neural policies for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF), which map local observations to action distributions, represents an important challenge in multi-agent learning, with practical relevance to scalable collective automation problems such as warehouse logistics. In contrast to prior studies focusing primarily on individual policy design, this study explores a meta-level Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approach to learning-based MAPF. Specifically, given a collection of compact yet high-performing experts specialised for different map distributions, our architecture learns a router that selectively fuses their outputs according to each agent's local situation. We instantiate and validate this MoE approach with a commonly used graph neural network-based policy as well as a newly developed recursive action-token refinement model. Combined with supervised and reinforcement learning fine-tuning of the experts, our experiments show that MoE generally improves upon the pretrained policy and outperforms existing leading methods. At the same time, our findings reveal that appropriately trained, parameter-matched monolithic models still outperform MoE, highlighting a nuanced role for map-distribution MoE for MAPF.

title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents
abstract: Long-horizon embodied agents face temporal confusion and incomplete or distorted records, recurring errors from fixed memory rules, and growing storage and retrieval costs. We present BetaMem, a framework for building and evolving traceable long-term memory through six linked layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural memory. A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Atomic tools frame storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost-utility allocation under storage and read budgets. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. Training the model for memory generation raises the contract pass rate from 50.9% to 86.2% while reducing output tokens per stored action by 47.3%. A separate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluation on EMem-Bench achieves an average success rate of 38.4% and an average error recurrence rate of 24.9%. We perform best among evaluated methods using comparably sized open-source models. Category results show that we have advantages in integrating information across observations, recalling events over long histories, and inferring personal habits.
triage_reason: neighbor: learns memory write operations with SFT plus RL under a write contract; recipe on benchmarks, cite in L4 learned-memory kill searches.

title: Adaptive Decoding Methods for Token-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Rollout decoding affects both which trajectories are used for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and how many completion tokens are spent collecting them. We study whether candidate-token support should remain fixed or widen during training in the context of rollout sampling efficiency. Our main schedule moves from top-K=10 to K=20 and then to full support as the attempted-token budget increases. In a 4B code-RLVR setting, the schedule has a higher interpolated 150M-token validation value than its matched fixed-K=10 continuation in all three runs, with a mean gain of $1.80{\pm}0.42$ points. The schedule also performs comparably to a separately trained fixed-K=20 baseline, the strongest fixed-support setting in our sweep. Follow-up experiments suggest that late widening to full support is the most promising variant, although the evidence remains noisy, and mixed-reward-group diagnostics do not clearly explain the gain. An exploratory single-run test replay yields identical point estimates for the schedule and fixed $K=10$. Overall, our results show that rollout support is an important control for sampling efficiency in RLVR and motivate further study of adaptive support schedules.
triage_reason: Top-K widening schedule for rollout sampling in 4B code RLVR; small noisy recipe gain, no systems or cost measurement.

title: A GPU-Resident Pipeline for Multi-Robot 3D Inspection with Limited Perception
abstract: We present a complete, GPU-resident pipeline for multi-robot 3D inspection of underwater structures. Given a triangle mesh and a fleet of $K$ robots, each carrying a short-range, limited field-of-view camera, the pipeline computes 6-DOF trajectories that jointly cover a target fraction of the surface while minimizing a linearly interpolated makespan/total-cost objective. The joint problem is NP-hard, so we decompose it into five core stages - candidate viewpoint generation, visibility computation, set cover, min-max vehicle routing solved as a mixed integer program (MIP) with lifted Miller-Tucker-Zemlin subtour elimination, and priority-based multi-agent path finding with continuous-time inter-robot conflict checking - flanked by mesh loading and surface sampling as preprocessing and by trajectory smoothing as postprocessing. Our contributions are: an end-to-end GPU-accelerated integration of the five stages, with its kernel design documented; a GPU batch adaptation of Lien's $\varepsilon$-visibility with four custom CUDA kernels; a $β$-aware per-vehicle tour upper bound derived from the interpolated objective, supplementing the Desrochers-Laporte coefficient lift with forbidden-pair cuts; a 4D space-time extension of Zhou and Zeng's GPU parallel-frontier A*; and an experimental evaluation on 14 meshes (up to $7.2$M faces) that ablates the routing cuts and the parallel-frontier search, audits collision freedom and waypoint attainment \emph{after} trajectory smoothing, and measures the end-to-end gap against analytical and LP-relaxation lower bounds. Code and raw results are publicly available.

title: Latent Projection for Latent Planning
abstract: Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the $\ell_2$ distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no signal. We show that the same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss-Markov process, the transition is linear with its covariance pinned by the map itself, $z' \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(Az,\, I - AA^\top)$. Fitting the state dynamics $A$ therefore yields the covariance at no additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining $A$ to be a normal matrix fixes that basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the planning cost on. We then restrict the $\ell_2$ cost to the $k$-dimensional subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, $A$, is fit. We evaluate across six environments and show large gains on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over the plain $\ell_2$ cost by up to $+54.7$ points under a harder planning setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.

title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
abstract: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.

title: Anatomy of Off-Policy Policy Gradient: Importance Sampling, KL Regularization, and Baselines
abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central tool for large language model (LLM) post-training, where policy gradient methods are routinely deployed off-policy, even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling. We study when such off-policy deployment is justified, and what roles its core ingredients, including importance sampling, KL regularization, and baselines, play in handling the resulting distribution shift. We show that for a general class of off-policy policy gradient updates, consistency, in the sense that the optimal policy remains a stationary point, requires one of two structures at the optimal policy: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from the well-known curse of horizon, or KL regularization with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value, instantiated by the grouped mean. Focusing on the KL route, we identify it with the group-relative policy gradient (GRPG) update, establish an equivalence to a trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization objective, and obtain a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage. This also gives a theoretical account of a variant of the empirically successful GRPO objective. We further uncover a hidden role of baselines in the off-policy setting: a constant shift in the baseline implements pessimism, the standard remedy in offline RL for partial data coverage. We instantiate this via the asymmetric REINFORCE objective, and connect it to the game-theoretic offline RL framework, showing a regret bound with single-policy coverage. Together, these results offer a unified theoretical view of off-policy policy gradient in LLM post-training and connect it to classical ideas in offline RL.
triage_reason: Theory of off-policy GRPO consistency and baselines as pessimism; single-turn recipe analysis, no credit signal checked against ground truth.

title: CUA-Lite: An Open Platform for Computer Use Agents
abstract: Open resources for computer use agents (CUAs) -- environments, datasets, and models -- remain scattered: without a standard, these resources cannot be integrated and scaled; additionally, evaluation, RL, and SFT cannot share one infrastructure. We present CUA-Lite, an open platform for developing CUAs, built around three standardized abstractions: (1) Unified environment interface, under which we integrate 12 benchmarks across desktop, browser, and mobile, plus lightweight VM-free sandboxes that replicate OSWorld's desktop at much lower cost, providing over 30,000 verifiable tasks. (2) Unified supervised data format, into which we convert the major public CUA datasets, from GUI grounding and understanding to full rollouts, and record our fresh rollouts from frontier CUAs on these verifiable environments. (3) Model harnesses shared across evaluation, RL, and SFT, one per model and implemented for 14 model families. Each harness runs its model in these computer environments, producing the rollouts that evaluation and RL consume, or renders stored supervised data into the model's own training format for SFT. We release reference scores across the integrated benchmarks, and show that RL and SFT through the same harness improve open-weight models. We release our dataset, code, and models, and the platform is open to contributions.

title: EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and Interactive World Models
abstract: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.

title: More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term this feedback mechanism error reproduction: errors are regenerated through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge. We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence in memorybased self-improvement.

title: ProMemAgent: Long-Horizon Proactive Assistance with Context-Aware Prospective Memory from Sensory Perceptions
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving beyond reactive responses toward proactive assistance that anticipates user needs without explicit requests. However, existing proactive agents primarily address immediate needs, while many everyday situations involve delayed intentions that can only be acted on hours or days later. Humans handle such intentions through prospective memory, the ability to remember to act on an intention when the right moment arises. In this paper, we introduce ProMemAgent, the first proactive agent to incorporate prospective memory over everyday sensory contexts for long-horizon proactive assistance. ProMemAgent organizes past sensory perceptions (e.g., egocentric video and audio) into context-aware memory, generating prospective cues and linking earlier events with subsequent developments for future retrieval. Given the current context, it retrieves relevant past events and performs memory-augmented proactive reasoning to determine whether assistance is needed. We further introduce CPMBench, the first benchmark for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance over sensory contexts, comprising 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories. Extensive experiments show that ProMemAgent achieves the best memory retrieval performance and consistently outperforms all baselines on long-horizon proactive assistance.

title: AutoRedClaw: Automated Red-Teaming for Claw-Style Agents
abstract: Agent systems are shifting from task-scoped tool-use agents to persistent, personalized assistants such as OpenClaw. These claw-style agents maintain configuration files (e.g., AGENTS.md), long-term memory, and reusable skills. Once poisoned, this persistent state is repeatedly reloaded into the agent's context, creating persistent threats across tasks and sessions. Existing security evaluation systems struggle to evaluate these complex claw-style systems since they rely heavily on manually constructed test cases and environments, which limits their scale and coverage; in addition, these manually designed cases quickly become outdated as agents evolve, and their evaluation settings leave a gap with how claw-style agents are deployed in practice. To address this, we introduce AutoRedClaw, an automated red-teaming framework that generates end-to-end attacks together with the environments needed to execute them. AutoRedClaw combines a strict quality-checking protocol with execution-based validation to ensure the correctness, realism, and effectiveness of generated samples, and adopts task-driven environment construction to keep costs low. To achieve broad coverage, it organizes generation along risk categories, attack strategies, attack stages, and attack surfaces, and uses experience-guided exploration to steer generation toward under-explored regions. AutoRedClaw achieves an effective attack rate above 30% at less than $0.10 per successful sample. From its outputs, we construct RedClaw-Bench, a 330-case benchmark that yields substantially higher attack success rates (ASRs) than AgentDojo, AgentDyn, and DTap. Across seven harnesses and four frontier models, most agent systems exceed 50% ASR, showing that our red-teaming pipeline provides a strong evaluation signal even for the most advanced agent systems. Our code and benchmark are released at https://github.com/SaFo-Lab/AutoRedClaw.

title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
abstract: Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate number actually represents. We release EGI-BENCH, a unified LLM agent benchmark suite that consolidates eight enterprise facing agent benchmarks (CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP-UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE, LOCOBENCH) behind a single command-line interface with two runtime-budgeted execution modes. On top of the suite we define the Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score, a six-dimensional framework (M1-M6) whose buckets are populated by fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark rather than by benchmark-level averages. We describe the suite, the sub-metric routing, and the quick/deep budgets, and report results for fourteen frontier and cost-efficient LLMs spanning the GPT, Claude, and Gemini families under quick mode. Top-line EGI ranges from 39.6 (GPT-4o mini) to 65.6 (gpt-5.5), and no single model dominates every capability axis: gpt-5.5 leads task outcome, planning, and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; and Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi-bench.

title: PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents act on the external world through tools and third-party skills, so a single executed action can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses judge a proposed action without tracking whether its content comes from the user or from external sources such as tool outputs, and they judge it in isolation rather than against an available alternative, which forces a trade-off between security and utility. We present PROVISO, a controller that decides which action to commit after the agent proposes an action and before it is executed. PROVISO encodes trusted observations, external observations, the proposed action, and an alternative into provenance-typed memory, relates them through role-specific queries, and commits the action with the highest calibrated value learned from outcomes. On four agent security tasks spanning the agent lifecycle, no baseline exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility. PROVISO improves F1 over the strongest baseline by 13.84 points on SkillsBench and by 7.07 points on ToolSafe, and it reaches 88-99 F1 on three additional skill detection benchmarks.

title: Embodied Playground: A Long-Horizon Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Physical, Strategic, and Spatial Reasoning
abstract: Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons. https://winniechen2002.github.io/Agent-bench-website/

title: GLOBE: Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit via Unit-Sphere Trajectories
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve problem solving, but models often keep generating after the correct answer is already reachable; the extra steps raise serving costs and may replace a correct intermediate result with an incorrect one. We propose GLOBE (Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit), an online, training-free algorithm that terminates the model's CoT process early. GLOBE embeds each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere and reads the shape of the resulting semantic trajectory. GLOBE first applies a trial phase that generates short trial answers in a separate branch, stopping the main stream on an accepted trial after checking confidence against a threshold. If generation continues, a trajectory phase stops the stream once this path repeatedly reverses direction with little net progress. On five benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, tool calling, and agent memory, GLOBE cuts output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time (E2E) by 51.0% across two models, and achieves a five-task average of 80.58%, comparable to Full CoT.

title: ACE-Trader: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Generator-Critic Trading Systems
abstract: Generator--critic trading systems pair an LLM-based trader that makes trading decisions with a red team agent that evaluates these decisions and provides feedback for revision. However, improving individual trading decisions does not ensure that both agents learn from experience and improve together over time. This raises an important question: how can the trader and red-Team select useful experience and learn from each other's evolving behavior? On one hand, experience that benefits decisions under one market condition may become ineffective or harmful under another. On the other hand, trading outcomes reflect both agents' actions, making it difficult to derive appropriate experience for each role. In this work, we propose ACE-Trader, an adversarial co-evolution trading framework. Specifically, we first develop separate context-dependent memory selectors that learn to identify useful experience for the current trading decision. Both selectors receive shared feedback from net-return differences between complete memory-assisted and memory-free trading pipelines, with online updates emphasizing recent outcomes. We further design a co-evolution mechanism that links role-specific memories through shared trading records. We use these records to evaluate the Red-Team's risk assessments and the effects of the Trader's revisions against realized market outcomes, then derive experience for their respective memories. By linking this experience to the corresponding records, we enable the Trader to improve its proposals based on prior critiques and the Red-Team to adjust its review focus as the Trader's behavior changes. Experiments on U.S. stock trading show that ACE-Trader outperforms all 22 active baselines in cumulative return and achieves the highest Sharpe ratio and lowest maximum drawdown across both active methods and passive benchmarks.

title: CoMem: Learning to Anticipate Failures from Retrieved Experience
abstract: Reflection lets LLM agents improve from their own attempts, but the memory it builds is local to a single task, so an agent reflecting on its own tends to revisit the same explanation for failure. Cross-task reflective memory addresses this in two forms: retrieved memory keeps past experience explicit and looks up related cases, which is specific but bounded by the bank, and parametric memory internalizes experience into parameters, which generalizes but is grounded in nothing beyond the task description. When both are used, existing agents combine them additively, feeding their outputs to the solver side by side, so retrieved experience never changes what the learned memory produces. We introduce CoMem (Compounding Memory), which makes retrieved experience an input to the learned memory itself, at training and at inference. The agent builds a bank of its own successful and failed reflections, learns from retrieved cases to write failure hypotheses, candidate explanations of how an attempt is likely to go wrong, and at test time reasons from newly retrieved cases to guide each attempt.
